title: Sell Mineral Rights in Alabama
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Alabama | Royalty Buyer
metaDescription: Get an Alabama mineral rights offer from a buyer who reads Black Warrior coalbed methane statements for a living. Free review, no obligation to sell.
heroLead: If your check comes out of Tuscaloosa, Fayette, or Walker County, it is almost certainly a coalbed methane gas check, and that changes how you should think about selling.
intro: The Black Warrior basin is one of the oldest coalbed methane fields in the country, and it does not behave like a shale play. Wells were drilled mostly through the 1990s and early 2000s to dewater the coal seams and release trapped gas, and most of that drilling is long finished. What is left is a mature, slow-decline gas field with thousands of small royalty owners scattered across west-central Alabama, many of them heirs to interests their grandparents signed decades ago.

Oil & Gas Royalty Buyer brings years of operating-side experience with CBM production curves, and Alabama's are gentler than a shale well's cliff but they still trend one direction. That matters when you are deciding whether the check you get every month is worth more to you now, as a lump sum, than it will be worth stretched out over the next ten or fifteen years of gradual decline.

sections.heading: Why an Alabama CBM Check Reads the Way It Does
paragraphs: Open a Black Warrior royalty statement and you will usually see one product code, not two. These are gas wells, produced water is a constant operating cost, and dewatering pumps are billed back against the well long after the coal seam has given up its early gas rush. That is a normal line item on these statements, not a sign something is wrong.

Deductions on Alabama gas checks tend to run heavier than on an oil check because gathering, compression, and dehydration all get subtracted before your royalty is calculated. If your net number looks small against the gross production volume printed above it, that gap is usually gathering and compression, not an error.

sections.heading: The Decline Curve You're Actually Sitting On
paragraphs: Most Black Warrior CBM wells hit their peak gas rate years ago and have been declining at a slow, steady rate since. That is the nature of coal seam gas: no sudden cliff like a shale well, but also very little chance of a workover or infill well bringing a surprise increase. Operators in this basin are not drilling many new wells against these older units.

That combination, mature production with almost no new drilling upside, is exactly the situation where selling the income stream can make more sense than holding it. You are not giving up on a play about to take off. You are converting a shrinking, steady trickle into a number you control today.

sections.heading: Heirship and Small Tracts Are the Norm Here
paragraphs: A large share of Alabama mineral owners we talk to inherited a fractional interest from a parent or grandparent who signed a lease decades before coalbed methane was even a common term. Interests get divided among siblings and cousins over a generation or two, and by the time it reaches you, the tract might represent a small percentage of a unit spread across several heirs.

That is not a disqualifier for selling. It just means the offer reflects your specific decimal interest, and we will walk through the division order with you so you understand exactly what percentage you own before any number gets discussed.

sections.heading: What Actually Happens if You Decide to Sell
paragraphs: We start with your last few royalty statements, not a guess. Production history, the operator's reported decline, and current gas pricing all factor into how an offer gets built, and the range depends heavily on how the specific well or unit has been performing recently rather than any flat statewide number.

From there it is a straightforward transfer: a mineral deed, a title check against the county courthouse records in the county where your interest sits, and a closing timeline that usually runs a few weeks. You keep any payments that were already earned before closing; we take on the well's future decline from that point forward.

faqs.question: Why does your Alabama gas check vary so much month to month?
faqs.answer: Gas price swings hit CBM checks harder than the underlying production volume does, since these wells produce a fairly steady gas rate. A cold winter spike or a summer price dip can move your check noticeably even when the well itself barely changed.

faqs.question: Is Black Warrior basin production still being drilled?
faqs.answer: New drilling in the basin has slowed to a trickle compared to the 1990s and early 2000s buildout. Most current activity is workovers and dewatering pump maintenance on existing wells rather than new units, which is part of why the decline curve is so predictable.

faqs.question: Is a small fractional interest worth selling?
faqs.answer: Small fractional interests are common in Alabama because of generational heirship, and they can still be sold. The offer is simply scaled to your decimal interest as shown on the division order, so a small percentage means a smaller number, not a declined offer.

faqs.question: Do you need a lawyer to sell your mineral rights in Alabama?
faqs.answer: You are not required to have one, but for larger or contested interests it is worth having an attorney review the mineral deed before you sign, particularly if the interest passed through an estate that was never formally probated.

faqs.question: How is your offer different from what your neighbor got?
faqs.answer: Offers are built off the specific well or unit's recent production and decline, plus your exact decimal interest, so two neighbors on different wells within the same field can reasonably get different numbers even in the same county.
